summary: STORY: Nvidia’s H200 AI chip sales to China are in question due to a pending U.S. national security review. That’s according to the Financial Times Tuesday (February 3), citing sources. It comes almost two months after U.S. President Donald Trump approved the tech giant’s exports. Meanwhile, the report said, Chinese customers aren't placing orders for the powerful H200 chip with Nvidia. They’re waiting for clarity on whether they’ll be able to secure licenses - or the conditions that could be attached. Reuters couldn't immediately verify the report. Nvidia and the U.S. State Department didn't immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.In January, the Commerce Department eased export curbs on the H200 for China.But it required license applications to be reviewed by the U.S. departments of State, Defense and Energy.According to the FT, the Commerce Department has completed its analysis but the State Department was pushing for tougher restrictions...With its goal being to make it harder for China to use the H200 chips in ways that would undermine U.S. national security.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week his firm's license to sell the chip in the country is being finalized.Reuters reported last month that China had approved its first batch of H200 chips for import.It marks a shift for Beijing as it tries to balance its AI needs against pushing domestic development.

Nvidia-backed CoreWeave also slid nearly 6%.AI will remain in the spotlight, with five of the Magnificent Seven megacap firms reporting quarterly earnings this week.Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, said he's expecting strong results."What I think we are more than likely to find out is that the demise of software has been vastly overstated. Again, the scalability of AI is limited to who owns the compute. And right now it's the really large hyperscalers that have all of the data. [FLASH] Coming through this week and all of the Mag 7 earnings, our expectation is that we're probably going to see that the capex numbers are pretty much the same, maybe even a little bit higher because of the lack of compute that's out there. And also the fact that they are still seeing contract sales go up because they can scale at an enterprise-wide system much more cost efficiently than you can just going directly to generative AI in this moment.":: ArchiveMeanwhile, the Federal Reserve convened for what is likely Jerome Powell's last monetary policy meeting as chair of the central bank.While the Fed is likely to leave interest rates unchanged on Wednesday, the accompanying statement and Powell's subsequent press conference will be parsed for views on inflation and the related spike in oil prices due to the U.S. war in Iran.

headline: Samsung chip profit jumps almost 50-fold; supply shortage to worsen
summary: STORY: Samsung reported record quarterly profit on Thursday driven by a 49-fold jump in chip income.The South Korean tech giant said January-March operating profit in its chip division reached a record $36.15 billion.It was massively up from a year before and represented 94% of the quarter's total.Overall revenue rose 69% on the year to $90.4 billion.It marks a positive step for the firm which wants to close the gap with rival SK Hynix in supplying high bandwidth memory chips to Nvidia.SK Hynix last week reported record quarterly profit following a fivefold jump in earnings.The chipmakers have seen a boom in the construction of AI data centers.It's led firms to allocate production capacity to advanced chips Nvidia uses in its so-called AI accelerators.Chipmakers have struggled to meet demand while the move also squeezes the supply of conventional semiconductors.Samsung said Thursday - quote - its supply falls far short of customer demand.And it believes the supply-to-demand gap for 2027 is due to widen even further than this year.The firm said continued development in AI tech will lead to sustained demand growth.But supply will stay constrained for the time being due to the lead time required for new factory construction.Elsewhere, Samsung said conflict in the Middle East hasn't disrupted chipmaking.It cited secured inventory and diversified sources of gases used in manufacturing.But it warned there's a risk of higher transportation costs caused by rising oil prices.Samsung also faces possible production disruption as unions representing the majority of its workers in South Korea could strike over pay.Samsung said it "plans to respond to the fullest extent to ensure production isn't disrupted."Shares of the firm slipped almost 2.5% Thursday after rising as much as 1.8% following the earnings announcement.The stock has surged 88% this year.
